title: The friend who includes
description: Inclusion is rarely a speech. It is a chair moved, a name remembered, an invitation repeated.

body.heading: Watch the edges
paragraphs: Every group has edges: the person standing slightly outside the circle, the colleague eating alone, the cousin nobody has briefed on the family joke. Including them starts with simply noticing — a skill that improves the moment you decide to practise it.
You were on an edge once, or will be. Memory is a good teacher here.

body.heading: Make the invitation specific
paragraphs: “You should join us sometime” is kind but weightless. “We’re walking to the market at twelve — come” can actually be accepted. Specific invitations name a time, a place, and an easy exit, which is exactly what an uncertain person needs.
And invite twice. A first refusal often means “I wasn’t sure I was really wanted,” not “no.” The second invitation is the one that proves the first was real.

body.heading: Share the map
paragraphs: Inside jokes, unwritten rules, who is who — newcomers lack the map everyone else navigates by. Narrating it lightly (“We always order too much; it’s tradition”) turns an audience into participants.
The friend who includes rarely gets thanked dramatically. They get something better: rooms that relax when they enter them.

takeaway: Notice the edges, invite specifically and twice, and hand newcomers the map.
